items.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: And of course at that time there were still Tommy Dorsey’s “Boogie Woogie,” and Benny Goodman and a few others.

ctx.x: The bebop at the time was a little more challenging for the listener, it kind of abandoned the dance end of things. Did it have any effect on your listening do you suppose?
Well I don’t know. I guess I didn’t listen too much to it because I really enjoyed this swing and I think even going, when we got into high school we used to have noontime © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

dances in high school. It was five days a week. The Student Council would charge two cents admission and with that money that they’d collect every day, once a week we’d go out and buy records. And of course at that time there were still Tommy Dorsey’s “Boogie Woogie,” and Benny Goodman and a few others. So in addition to the pop singers in the early 50s, because I was president of the Student Council, I’d go out and buy some jazz records, and kids were dancing every noontime in the gym.
